newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bond market faces risk of delivery failure.
newsitem.headline: Japan bond market faces risk of delivery failure.

text.p: Japan's bond market is facing the startling prospect that some players may fail to deliver bonds at settlement because some U.S. hedge funds tried to corner the market, bond traders said on Tuesday.
Failure to deliver bonds is strictly forbidden in Japan's settlement system, unlike many other countries where failure is overlooked if a fine is paid.

The bonds some market players might fail to deliver, the target of apparent short-squeezing by U.S. hedge funds, are the 161st, 163rd and to a lesser extent 164th 10-year JGBs (Japanese government bonds).
They are the cheapest JGBs which can be delivered against September JGB futures contracts, which expired last Friday.
A record 2.3519 trillion yen ($21.5 billion) worth of the September contract is due for settlement through delivery of cash JGBs, the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) said.

Traders said Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd looks likely to receive much of the cash delivery against the September contract and U.S. hedge funds could be behind the major U.S. brokerage. A spokeswoman for the company declined to comment.
One official at the Ministry of Finance (MOF) told Reuters the ministry is closely monitoring the situation.

While an exceptionally large amount of cash JGBs are due for delivery, there is a severe shortage of the cheapest deliverable cash JGBs, traders said. Cash delivery of the September contract is scheduled for Friday next week.
Those who had sold the September contract would find it expensive to deliver bonds other than the cheapest JGBs.
They often acquire them by borrowing from the repo market (lending market) but repo rates for these JGBs were extremely high last week.

The repo rate for the 161st went above 10 percent of face value at one point. On Tuesday, it was five percent, still high compared with 0.2-0.3 percent a month earlier. The 161st and 163rd JGBs are in short supply, with the outstanding amount in the market about 800 billion yen ($7.33 billion) each, together still less than the open interest in September JGB futures.
One trader said U.S. hedge funds, thought to have long positions on the September futures contract, were borrowing heavily at the same time, and their activity led to the shortage of cheapest JGBs.

He estimated the hedge funds had borrowed about 500 billion yen ($4.58 billion) worth of the 161st JGBs, on top of their long position of about 150 billion yen ($1.37 billion) in the same issue. They also borrowed about 500 billion yen ($4.58 billion) worth of the 163rd JGBs and may have bought roughly a net 250 billion yen ($2.29 billion) worth in addition, the trader added.
The calculation suggests the hedge funds have an enormous amount of the cheapest JGBs, nearly cornering the market.

A TSE official said: "We do not expect a failure of deliveries for the September as a wide range of JGBs are still available in the cash market." Deliverable cash bonds for any futures contract are JGBs which have more than seven years but less than 11 years to maturity, as of settlement.
But traders said strong demand for those JGBs lingers on even after the settlement, ahead of many Japanese firms' half-year book-closing at the end of September.

"The current focus is whether those who need to borrow bonds for delivery against the September will be able to roll over the repo agreement at the end of September," said a senior trader at a major local brokerage.

If those bond borrowers are unable to extend their borrowing contracts due to lenders' reluctance or due to higher repo rates, there is a risk that delivery may fail, traders said. "If the hedge funds are not going to let these bonds go, somebody must fail,...it all depends on them," said the first trader. ($1=109 yen)
